365.title: Ki Tisa: even the sanctuary rests (Exodus 31:12–17)
365.hook: the building work stops for Shabbat; these verses are sung on Friday night
365.tomorrow: Ki Tisa: show me thy glory
365.howItsDone: V'shamru (Exodus 31:16–17) is sung in the Friday evening service, and in some communities it is also recited before the kiddush on Shabbat morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God. Your line was craft is spirit. Today, all that work stops.

The biggest project in the camp is about to begin: a home for God. The plans have come down from the mountain, the gold has been collected, the best artist in the camp has been named. Everyone is eager. And the very next thing the Torah says, right after naming Bezalel, is: stop. Not forever. Every seventh day. Even this building, holy work, puts its tools down for Shabbat. And the verses that say so are sung in synagogues on Friday night.
screen: `A HOME FOR GOD.` → `RIGHT AFTER BEZALEL: STOP.` → `SUNG EVERY FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The passage begins with v'shamru, and they shall keep. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant." It calls Shabbat a sign between God and Israel forever, because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day ceased from work and rested. The rabbis noticed where this sits: right after all the instructions for the sanctuary. Rashi says the point is plain: however eager you are to build, the building does not push Shabbat aside. The Talmud goes further. When the rabbis listed the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat, thirty-nine of them, they drew the list from the work of building the sanctuary: sowing, weaving, writing, building, kindling, and the rest. The labors that made a home for God are exactly the labors that stop on God's day. One more word. When the verse says God rested, the Hebrew is vayinafash, and Rashi hears in it nefesh, soul or breath. He reads it as catching one's breath, getting one's soul back. Even the Creator, in the Torah's picture, pauses to breathe. V'shamru is sung in the Friday evening service, and in some communities it is said again before the Shabbat morning kiddush over wine.

Notice what comes, relief, worry, guilt, and breathe out slowly, the way vayinafash pictures it. If you keep Shabbat, picture this week's; if not, picture a few hours.
V'shamru. And they shall keep: the verses about keeping Shabbat, placed right after the sanctuary plans, and sung on Friday night.

366.title: Ki Tisa: show me thy glory (Exodus 33:18–23)
366.hook: Moses asks to see God, and sees only from behind, from a cleft in the rock
366.howItsDone: This passage, Exodus 33:12–34:26, is also the Torah reading for the Shabbat during Passover and Sukkot, so in some years Moses' request is heard again on those festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'shamru: even the holy building stops for Shabbat. Your line was even the temple rests. Today, Moses asks for something bold.

Between yesterday's verses and today's, the story has broken apart. While Moses was on the mountain, the people made a golden calf. Moses came down, saw them dancing, and broke the tablets of stone. Then came the long climb back: pleading for the people, pitching a tent outside the camp, speaking with God face to face, the text says, as a man speaks to his friend. And now Moses asks for one more thing. He wants to see God.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CALF.` → `THE TABLETS BROKEN.` → `ONE MORE REQUEST: SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation, it's one short line: "Show me, I pray Thee, Thy glory." God's answer comes in layers. First, a yes: I will make all My goodness pass before you, and call out My name. Then a no: you cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live. Then a way through. There's a place by Me, God says: stand on the rock. I'll put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand while I pass by. And then: "I will take away My hand, and thou shalt see My back; but My face shall not be seen." So Moses, who spoke with God as a man speaks to his friend, sees only from behind. What does that mean? The Torah doesn't explain, and Jewish readers have taken it in different ways. The Talmud, in Berakhot, says God showed Moses the knot of the tefillin at the back of the head: a picture, not a portrait. Maimonides says the face means God's essence, which no mind can grasp, and the back means God's ways in the world, which can be learned. And some readers hear something quieter: a person rarely sees God coming, only where God has been. Only looking back, at a hard year, a rescue, a meeting that changed everything, does someone sometimes say: there. That was it.

segments.voice: Think of a time that was hard while you were in it, and without reliving the worst, walk forward from there in your mind to now. Who showed up, what held, what turned out differently than you feared? If you pray, say thank you for it; if not, just let yourself see it.
Ki Tisa. The portion of the golden calf, the broken tablets, and Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing God only from behind.
Your line: seen only from behind. A rock to stand on, a hand over his eyes, and the view from behind. See you tomorrow.

367.title: Ki Tisa: the thirteen attributes (Exodus 34:6–7)
367.hook: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering", chanted on holy days
367.howItsDone: The thirteen attributes are chanted when the ark is opened on festivals in some communities, throughout the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days, on fast days, and again and again on Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses in the cleft of the rock. Your line was seen only from behind. Today, what Moses heard as God passed by.

On a festival morning, as the doors of the ark open and the Torah scroll is about to come out, some congregations stop and sing the same words three times over. On Yom Kippur the words return again and again, through the day, until the closing service. No rabbi composed them. They come from Exodus: the words Moses heard in the cleft of the rock, as God passed by. Moses asked to see. What he got was something to hear.
screen: `THE ARK OPENS.` → `THE SAME WORDS, THREE TIMES.` → `WHAT MOSES HEARD.`

segments.voice: Moses has carved two new tablets and climbed back up the mountain. God descends in the cloud, passes before him, and calls out. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." It goes on: keeping mercy to the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin. Jewish tradition counts these as the thirteen attributes of mercy; commentators divide the phrases in slightly different ways, but the count of thirteen holds. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah, imagines God here wrapped in a prayer shawl like a leader of the service, showing Moses an order of prayer, and saying: whenever Israel sins, let them say this before Me, and I will forgive. So after the golden calf, the people are given words to come back with. In the synagogue, there's a twist. In the Torah, verse seven goes on to say God will by no means clear the guilty. The prayer stops mid-sentence, just before that line, so it ends on the word for clearing, for cleansing. The Talmud, in Yoma, reads the verse's two halves together: God clears those who return, and does not clear those who don't. And another Talmudic passage, in Shabbat, reads these qualities as a pattern for people: as God is gracious and merciful, so you be gracious and merciful.

segments.voice: Let the list pass slowly through your mind: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, true, forgiving. Pick the one you've had least of lately, and picture meeting one person who tests it, a child, a coworker, yourself, with that quality, just once. 368.title: Vayakhel: he gathered them (Exodus 35:1)
368.hook: after the golden calf, Moses gathers everyone together again
368.howItsDone: Jewish communal life is organized around the kehillah, and certain prayers, such as the Kaddish, Barchu and the public Torah reading, are traditionally said only with a minyan of ten.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirteen attributes, the words Moses heard as God passed by. Your line was merciful and gracious. Today, a new portion, and an old verb.

A word in this week's portion turned up a few chapters back, at a dark moment. When Moses was late coming down the mountain, the people crowded around Aaron and demanded a god to go before them. The JPS translation says "the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron". That gathering made a golden calf. Now Moses is down, with new tablets, and the first thing he does in this portion uses the same Hebrew verb. Same people. Same root. A completely different kind of gathering.
screen: `A CROWD AROUND AARON.` → `THE GOLDEN CALF.` → `NOW, THE SAME VERB AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The portion is named for its first word, vayakhel, and he assembled. In the JPS 1917 translation: "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel." The root is three Hebrew letters, kuf, hey, lamed, and it means to gather people into one body. From that same root comes today's word, kehillah, a community. Tradition calls a Jewish town's organized community its kehillah, and sometimes a kehillah kedoshah, a holy community. The book of Ecclesiastes is called Kohelet in Hebrew, a name traditionally read as the gatherer, from the same root. Now set the two gatherings side by side. The first time, the people gather themselves against their leader, out of fear and impatience, and make an idol. This time, Moses gathers all of them, and the first thing he tells them about is Shabbat: six days of work, a seventh of rest. Then he asks for gifts for the sanctuary, from everyone whose heart is willing. Some commentators hear a repair in this: the same energy that built a calf can build a sanctuary. A crowd isn't good or bad by itself. What matters is what it gathers around. Jewish prayer keeps that idea close: certain prayers are said only with a minyan, ten gathered together.

segments.voice: Think of people around you who don't see each other enough: neighbors, cousins, old friends. Picture what could bring a few of them together for something good, a meal, a walk, a visit to someone lonely, and who would come. Keep it small and real, and sit with the picture of them in one room.

369.title: Vayakhel: too much (Exodus 36:5–7)
369.hook: the people bring so much that Moses asks them to stop
369.howItsDone: Jewish charity, tzedakah, is often given through communal funds, and the story of the overflowing gifts for the sanctuary is read each year in the portion Vayakhel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kehillah: Moses gathered the people again, this time for something good. Your line was gather the people. Today, they give.

Every fundraiser has the same worry: will enough come in? The school bake sale, the roof appeal, the online campaign with a little bar creeping toward the goal. Now picture the opposite. The gifts pour in so fast that the people running the project go to the leader and say, please, make them stop. There's too much. The Torah wrote down that it happened, in the desert, with a camp of former slaves building a sanctuary out of what they carried.
screen: `WILL ENOUGH COME IN?` → `PLEASE, MAKE THEM STOP.` → `IT HAPPENED IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Moses has asked for gifts for the sanctuary from everyone whose heart moves them: gold, silver, bronze, blue and purple yarn, linen, goat hair, wood, oil, spices, stones. The text says they kept bringing, morning after morning. Then the craftspeople stop their work and come to Moses: the people are bringing much more than enough. So Moses sends word through the whole camp: no man or woman should make anything more for the offering. And the Torah adds, so the people were held back from bringing. Then one last line, in the JPS 1917 translation: "For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much." In Hebrew, dayam v'hoter: their enough, and more. How can something be exactly sufficient and also too much? The eighteenth-century commentator Or HaChaim offers a tender answer: there really was extra, but God made room for all of it in the work, so that no one who gave would see their gift set aside. The Jerusalem Talmud adds a sharper note: this same people gave their gold for the calf, and gave their gold for the sanctuary. The generosity was the same. What changed was what it was for. And notice who says stop. Not the givers. The builders. It takes someone close to the work to see that the need is met, and the honesty to say so out loud, when it would be easy to keep taking.

370.title: Vayakhel: the women's mirrors (Exodus 38:8)
370.hook: the washing basin is made from women's copper mirrors; Rashi says God held them most dear
370.howItsDone: Rashi's midrash on the mirrors is a well-loved teaching on the portion Vayakhel, often cited to honor the women of the Exodus whose courage kept families alive in slavery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gifts so many that the builders said stop. Your line was they had to say stop. Today, one gift Moses almost refused.

Before glass mirrors, people looked at themselves in polished metal: a disk of copper or bronze, rubbed until it shone. In the desert, some Israelite women had mirrors like that. Small, personal things, the kind you might not think to give to a holy building. In the middle of a long list of what Bezalel made, the Torah stops for one sentence to say where the metal for a single object came from. The object is the washing basin. The metal came from those mirrors.
screen: `POLISHED COPPER MIRRORS.` → `SMALL, PERSONAL THINGS.` → `ONE SENTENCE IN A LONG LIST.`

segments.voice: The verse says Bezalel made the basin of bronze, and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the women who served at the door of the tent of meeting. The basin stood between the tent and the altar, and the priests washed their hands and feet in it before they served. The Torah says nothing more about who the women were or why they gave. Rashi fills the silence with a midrash. When the women brought their mirrors, Moses hesitated. These were made for vanity, he thought, for looking pretty. Then God said to him: accept them. These are dearer to Me than everything else. Why? Because of Egypt. The midrash says that when the men came home crushed from the slave labor, these women took their mirrors, sat beside their husbands, made them laugh and look again, and kept love alive. Families kept growing, even in slavery, and because of those mirrors, the midrash says, a people survived to leave. So, in the midrash, the very objects Moses nearly turned away became the basin the priests washed in before they served. A mirror shows you yourself. A basin of water is where you prepare to serve someone else. The same metal did both. And in Rashi's telling, the gift that looked least holy was the one God held dearest.

371.title: Vayakhel: wise-hearted spinners (Exodus 35:25–26)
371.hook: women whose hearts stirred them spun the goats' hair with skill
371.howItsDone: The Torah's phrase for a skilled craftsperson is wise of heart (chacham lev, or chachmat lev for a woman), and the women spinners of Exodus 35 are read about each year in the portion Vayakhel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women's bronze mirrors became the priests' basin. Your line was mirrors became the basin. Today, more women at work.

Goat hair is not glamorous. It's coarse, it smells like goat, and it's hard to work. But the sanctuary needed it: a tent of goat-hair cloth stretched over the beautiful inner curtains, taking the sun and the dust and the wind so the rest could stay fine. Somebody had to spin it into yarn. The Torah could have just said it was done. Instead, it stops to tell us who did it, and what moved them to do it.
screen: `COARSE, HARD-TO-WORK GOAT HAIR.` → `THE TENT OVER THE TENT.` → `WHO SPUN IT, AND HOW.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation: "And all the women that were wise-hearted did spin with their hands." They brought blue and purple and scarlet yarn, and fine linen. Then the next verse: "And all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun the goats' hair." Twice in two verses, wisdom sits in the heart. In Hebrew such a woman is chachmat lev, wise of heart, the Torah's phrase for a skilled person. The heart in biblical Hebrew is where people think and choose, not only where they feel. So a skilled hand starts in a wise heart. Rashi adds a detail from the Talmud that's hard to picture: these women spun the hair while it was still on the goats, and he calls it an exceptional art. The Torah never gives their names, but it credits them right there in the building story, alongside Bezalel and the craftsmen. Look back over this week: the building stopping for Shabbat, Moses in the cleft of the rock, the thirteen attributes, Moses gathering the people again, gifts so many the builders said stop, mirrors turned into a basin. And now, women spinning coarse hair with wise hearts, for the tent that would take the weather. The sanctuary isn't only gold. It's also goat hair, spun by people whose names we'll never know, and whose skill the Torah made sure to record.
screen: `WISE-HEARTED WOMEN SPUN.` · `CHACHMAT LEV: WISE OF HEART.` · `SPUN ON THE GOATS THEMSELVES.` · `CREDITED IN THE BUILDING STORY.` · then, large: `WISE HEARTS SPIN.`

segments.voice: Think of a person whose work holds things together without anyone noticing: the one who always knows where everything is, the one who calms a room. Picture their hands at work, and name the skill exactly, as if you were writing it into the Torah's list.
Vayakhel. The portion of the gathering, where wise-hearted women spin blue and purple yarn, and coarse goats' hair, for the sanctuary.
Your line: wise hearts spin. A skilled hand starts in a wise heart. See you tomorrow.
